For cancer subtyping, we evaluate NICER on two tasks: NSCLC subtyping on TCGA (2 classes), and ISUP grading on PANDA challenge (6 classes) ( Bulten et al., 2022 ; Bulten et al., 2020 ) . In survival prediction, we evaluate NICER with in-cohort TCGA-BRCA and TCGA-LUAD and cross-cohort evaluation with CPTAC. Following Song et al. (2024) , we evaluate the cancer subtyping tasks using Kappa ( Vieira et al., 2010 ) , weighted F1, accuracy for PANDA and balanced accuracy for NSCLC. For survival tasks, we report the concordance index (C-Index) ( Alabdallah et al., 2024 ) . Evaluation Settings. We evaluate NICER and baselines along two axes: (i) condensation ability, by applying NICER and baselines on the training set and testing against the original WSI feature bag; and (ii) morphological prototyping, by applying methods to both training and test sets. Baselines.

We consider two categories of baselines: (1) unsupervised prototyping methods, which preserve task-agnostic representations, and (2) MIL-based predictors, which learn supervised slide-level representations from the whole bag. For unsupervised prototyping, we use DeepSets ( Zaheer et al., 2017 ) , ProtoCounts ( Claudio Quiros et al., 2024 ) , H2T ( Yu et al., 2023 ) , InfiniteGPFA ( Yu et al., 2025a ) , Optimal Transport (OT) ( Mialon et al., 2021 ) , and PANTHER ( Song et al., 2024 ) . For MIL-based predictors, we adopt ABMIL ( Ilse et al., 2018 ) , DSMIL ( Li et al., 2021a ) , and ILRA ( Xiang and Zhang, 2023 ) . These models are either trained on condensed representations and evaluated on original feature bags to assess condensation quality, or used directly to evaluate NICER’s ability to produce unsupervised slide-level representations. On BRCA, NICER improves the C-index by up to 33.40% (4.98% on average), while on NSCLC it achieves gains of 2.82% and 4.70% with ABMIL and DSMIL, respectively. With the ILRA predictor, NICER surpasses the Whole-Bag upper bound on several tasks, suggesting that condensation can denoise or regularize representations for survival prediction. Results on survival prediction (Cross-cohort). We evaluate the generalizability of NICER in cross-cohort settings against multiple baselines. As shown in Tab. 1 , NICER consistently outperforms all baselines across diverse predictor architectures by approximately 5%. Moreover, NICER exhibits a substantially smaller performance gap between in-cohort evaluation on LUAD and cross-cohort evaluation on CPTAC compared to other methods, indicating that it learns transferable representations. 4.3 Performance on Morphological Prototyping As shown in Tab. 2 , NICER consistently outperforms other unsupervised methods across all scenarios, demonstrating its ability to preserve semantic information from the original noisy feature bag. Due to its nonparametric learning process and decomposition of diversity and compactness, NICER constructs representations that achieve competitive performance, exhibit only minimal drops across diverse tasks and datasets, underscoring its model-agnostic nature. In contrast, the performance of MIL methods is strongly dependent on the chosen architecture. Each pattern exhibits high intra-pattern morphological consistency, indicating that the condensed representations preserve fine-grained cellular and tissue-level features. Moreover, NICER is able to separate closely related but diagnostically distinct patterns (e.g., viable tumor versus tumor-adjacent necrosis), which are critical for pathological assessment. Implementation details and additional analysis are in App. L . Computation cost comparison. We compare the computational cost of NICER with the state-of-the-art PANTHER and the Whole Bag setting. As shown in Tab. 4 , both PANTHER and NICER reduce storage from 194GB to 3.2–5.7GB. While NICER incurs higher per-iteration GPU and runtime costs during condensation to preserve fine-grained representations, this modest overhead leads to substantially better downstream performance. Because condensation is performed once per WSI, the additional cost is amortized and negligible relative to the gains. More details are discussed in App. E . Impact of Initial Number of Patterns. Fig. 4 illustrates the effect of the number of patterns initialized at the start of the NICER algorithm on feature construction performance. Experiments are conducted on the PANDA dataset and evaluated on the Condensation Ability task using ABMIL as the predictor. As shown, NICER achieves substantial performance gains as the number of patterns increases, but the improvement begins to saturate beyond a certain point (e.g., ∼ \sim 200). This trend arises because a larger pattern set provides greater distillation capacity, while the plateau reflects the condensation process, which removes redundancy and converges toward stable representations. More results with different pretrained encoders and more extreme datasets can be found in App. K 6 Conclusions and Limitations Conclusion.

We reformulated whole-slide image condensation as a distribution-matching problem under a fixed representation lens and showed that it admits a principled nonparametric solution via Poisson point process–based MAP inference. This view naturally allows the number of condensed prototypes to adapt to the complexity of each slide and motivates NICER, a tractable learning-based framework for per-slide condensation. Experiments across multiple histopathology benchmarks, supported by pathological evaluation, demonstrate consistent improvements in efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, underscoring the benefits of a theoretically grounded approach to scalable WSI representation learning. Limitations. NICER has several limitations. First, it adopts a bag-of-features formulation and does not explicitly model spatial or multi-scale dependencies among patches, which may restrict its ability to capture fine-grained tissue organization in tasks where spatial context is important. Second, the PPP prior assumes independent concept occurrence, which may be insufficient for representing strongly correlated or highly complex morphological patterns. Finally, NICER operates on fixed pretrained representations. Although we evaluate two foundation models, a broader study across diverse encoders is needed to more fully characterize its robustness and generalizability across settings. We acknowledge such limitations in details in App. M . D.1 Datasets We provide brief explanations for the datasets that were used for the evaluation of NICER for condensation ability and prototyping ability. PANDA. [ 3 , 4 ] For the ISUP grading task, we used prostate cancer core needle biopses (n=10,616) from the Prostate Cancer Grade Assessment (PANDA) challenge. Each biopsy is given an ISUP grade, making this a 6-class classification task. These biopses are collected from Karolinska Institute (KRLS) and Radboud University Medical Center (RUMC).

We label-stratify the PANDA dataset into train/val/test of 80:10:10 and performance was evaluted using Cohen’s quadratic weighted Kappa κ 2 \kappa^{2} , accuracy and weighted F1 metrics. NSCLC. For the non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) subtyping task, we use H&E WSIs from TCGA for classifying lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) cases. The TCGA cohort contains a total of 1,041 slides (LUAD: 529, LUSC: 512). We label-stratify the TCGA cohort into train/val/test fold of 80:10:10 and evaluate performance using Cohen’s Kappa, balanced accuracy and F1 metrics. TCGA-BRCA. The Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) cohort from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). a joint effort of the NCI and NHGRI, provides one of the most comprehensive digital pathology resources for breast cancer. The dataset contains 1,133 diagnostic WSIs spanning 1,062 patients, covering diverse histological and molecular subtypes. In addition to imaging, the cohort supplies curated clinical outcomes, including Overall Survival (OS) and Progression-Free Interval (PFI), which have been widely adopted as endpoints for developing and benchmarking survival prediction models. We label-stratify the TCGA-BRCA dataset into train/val/test fold of 80:10:10 and evaluate performance C-Index for survival prediction TCGA-LUAD. The Lung Adenocarcinoma (LUAD) cohort within TCGA offers a large-scale, multi-institutional collection of pathology images and outcome data for a major subtype of non-small cell lung cancer. It includes 529 diagnostic WSIs corresponding to 478 patients, with extensive clinical annotation. As with BRCA, the LUAD cohort provides OS and PFI as standardized survival endpoints, enabling robust prognostic modeling and cross-study comparison in computational pathology research. We label-stratify the TCGA-LUAD dataset into train/val/test fold of 80:10:10 and evaluate performance C-Index for survival prediction CPTAC.

We use CPTAC as an external evaluation cohort to assess cross-cohort generalization on the survival prediction task. Models trained on the TCGA cohort are directly evaluated on CPTAC LUAD (185 patients, 486 WSIs) without further adaptation. This setting is substantially more challenging due to pronounced dataset shifts, including variations in image acquisition and H&E staining protocols, differences in geographic and demographic distributions (reflecting social determinants of health), and potential cohort-specific biases such as discrepancies in clinical follow-up and outcome annotation procedures between TCGA and CPTAC. D.2 Evaluation Setting Details We view unsupervised prototype construction not only as a condensation framework, whose primary role is to reduce redundancy in the WSI feature bag, but also as a form of representation learning, since the resulting prototypes are later used as inputs for downstream predictors. Accordingly, we evaluate all methods along two complementary axes: Condensation ability. Here, the goal is to assess how well the condensed prototype set preserves information from the original WSI feature bag. Specifically, we apply NICER and baseline methods on the training set to obtain prototypes, and then evaluate them on the original uncompressed bag of features. This setup isolates the effectiveness of condensation by measuring how much predictive power is retained (or lost) after summarization, independent of downstream task complexity. It answers the key question: Does condensation discard critical information or faithfully represent the original slide? Morphological prototyping. In this setting, we follow the prior evaluation protocol [ 48 ] to test whether condensed prototypes can generalize as useful, task-agnostic representations. Condensation methods are applied to both the training and test sets, and the resulting prototypes are directly used for downstream prediction.

Unlike the condensation ability evaluation, this setup emphasizes the representation learning capacity of the prototypes, focusing on whether they capture robust morphological cues transferable across unseen WSIs rather than reconstruction fidelity. To ensure fairness, we use a nonlinear transformer layer for all baselines since NICER produces prototype sets whose capacity adapts to WSI complexity and thus cannot be fully exploited by a fixed MLP layer. We extend the findings of Section 4.2 by examining additional WSI instances from TCGA-NSCLC. Figure 7 illustrates the trajectories of concept prototypes over 10 optimization iterations of NICER for three representative samples: TCGA-93-A4JN-01Z-00-DX1.ED4C9365-6CCF-4AEE-B4C9-3CC5EC57286C , TCGA-50-6594-01Z-00-DX1.43b2005a-4245-4025-ad85-4a957f308a5c , and TCGA-49-4514-01Z-00-DX2.f1565a36-257d-432e-a84d-47c1d7a0185f . The visualizations reveal that different WSIs exhibit distinct condensation dynamics, reflecting variation in morphological complexity and feature distribution. For example, the first sample (ending in “86C”) shows prototypes that initially cluster tightly, suggesting greater homogeneity, whereas the other two slides begin with more diffuse clusters, indicating higher heterogeneity. Figure 7 : 2D t-SNE visualizations of NICER’s concept prototypes learned over five iterations using three representative TCGA slides. These plots highlight that NICER can capture different diverse information across different WSIs.

Despite these sample-specific differences, a consistent pattern emerges across all trajectories: prototypes gradually diverge from their initialization with increasing variance, reflecting how condensation enforces specialization and reduces redundancy while preserving diversity. This behavior highlights NICER’s ability to uncover distinct and non-overlapping concept structures within each slide. Complementary evidence is shown in Figure 10 , where the number of prototypes stabilizes after only a few iterations. This rapid convergence indicates that redundant concepts are pruned early, leaving a compact and stable set that continues to refine qualitatively rather than quantitatively. Together, these results emphasize NICER’s efficiency in learning diverse, non-redundant representations of WSIs with minimal optimization steps. Figure 8 : 2D t-SNE visualization of original WSI feature bags and learned concept prototypes, comparing our method (NICER) with a representative prior approach (PANTHER). Diversity Preservation. To evaluate NICER’s ability to preserve diversity across whole-slide images (WSIs), we compare 2D t-SNE visualizations of concept prototypes generated by NICER and PANTHER, alongside the original feature bags, on three TCGA-NSCLC samples: TCGA-93-A4JN-01Z-00-DX1.ED4C9365-6CCF-4AEE-B4C9-3CC5EC57286C , TCGA-50-6594-01Z-00-DX1.43b2005a-4245-4025-ad85-4a957f308a5c , and TCGA-49-4514-01Z-00-DX2.f1565a36-257d-432e-a84d-47c1d7a0185f . For fair visualization, NICER’s prototypes are clustered with K-Means to 16, matching the fixed prototype count used in PANTHER [ 48 ] . As shown in Figure 8 , PANTHER fails to capture the inherent diversity of WSIs, collapsing heterogeneous regions into a limited number of clusters and discarding critical information required for downstream tasks, an effect consistent with its suboptimal performances in Table 1 and Table 2 .

This limitation arises because PANTHER enforces a rigid and heuristically small prototype budget, prioritizing efficiency at the expense of representational fidelity. In contrast, NICER employs an alternating optimization strategy that leverages pattern-based diversity preservation and condensation-driven efficiency, ensuring prototypes remain well-separated and encode distinct, slide-specific information. This balance enables NICER to adapt to the variability of individual WSIs while maintaining compact yet expressive concept sets. To validate the consistency of our observations in Fig. 8 , we further project the original feature bag and the concept prototypes learned by NICER and PANTHER for a WSI from the TCGA-BRCA cohort (slide ID: TCGA-49-4514-01Z-00-DX2.f1565a36-257d-432e-a84d-47c1d7a0185f ) using three 2D projection methods: t-SNE, UMAP, and PCA. As shown in Fig. 12 , NICER preserves a diverse set of pathological patterns after the condensation process. In contrast, PANTHER yields highly similar prototype representations with limited discriminative structure, indicating substantial information loss. This observation aligns with ours from Fig. 8 and downstream results shown in Sec. 4 . Concept Prototype Capacity Analysis . To evaluate NICER’s ability to adapt its capacity to complexity of data, we report the average number of concept prototypes across different datasets. As can be seen from Table 8 , for larger and more complex WSIs (e.g., NSCLC, LUAD, BRCA), NICER naturally allocates more capacity to preserve the underlying conceptual diversity in the slides. This aligns with our observation in Section 4 .

Extensive Results on Impacts of Number of Initial Prototypes ( M M ). Table 9 complements the analysis in Figure 4 by evaluating how the initial number of patterns influences NICER’s performance across different predictor architectures. The results demonstrate that increasing the pattern set size consistently improves performance, as a larger pool enhances the model’s capacity to distill informative representations. However, these gains diminish once the pattern set grows beyond a certain threshold, with performance gradually reaching a plateau.

This saturation reflects the role of the condensation process, which systematically eliminates redundancy and stabilizes the number of effective representations required to characterize a WSI, regardless of the starting pattern count, aligning our insights discussed from Figure 4 . Extensive Results on Impacts of Top- κ \kappa during Pattern Exploration. We further conduct a sensitivity analysis on the number of pattern assigned to each patch feature, controlled by the top- κ \kappa selection in the Condensation Ability tasks. The results, reported in Tab. 11 , reveal a clear trend: model performance improves steadily across all evaluation metrics as κ \kappa increases, indicating that incorporating multiple patterns per patch allows richer information to be preserved. However, beyond a moderate value (e.g., κ = 3 \kappa=3 ), this benefit begins to diminish, with performance gains plateauing or even slightly decreasing. The degradation at larger κ \kappa arises because information from each patch becomes overly dispersed across many patterns, weakening the sharpness of the distilled representation. These observations corroborate our earlier findings in Fig. 4 and Tab. 3 , and reinforce the design principle outlined in Sec. 3.1 that pattern assignments must balance informativeness with compactness. In both settings, NICER consistently outperforms both PANTHER and OT. This confirms that the performance gain indeed comes from NICER design rather than from leveraging more prototype budget. Notably, the results also show that the performance of PANTHER and OT do not increase with more prototype budget (see Tab. 12 ). This observation is consistent with prior work [ 48 ] , which reports that the performance of fixed-budget condensation methods does not necessarily improve with larger storage/prototype budgets and may even degrade. This is because a globally fixed budget cannot account for variations in slide complexity: it may allocate excessive capacity to simple slides while providing insufficient capacity for complex ones. This mismatch can introduce redundant or biased features in the former case and information loss in the latter, limiting transferability across tasks and prediction heads. These results highlight the need for a condensation framework with slide-adaptive capacity, such as NICER. K.1 Performance on a Needle-In-A-Hay-Stack Dataset Setup. First, NICER adopts a bag-of-features assumption, treating patches independently without explicitly modeling spatial or multi-scale relationships.

While this aligns with assumptions of standard MIL settings and is suitable for our tasks, fine-grained tissue architecture and spatial priors are not directly captured, which may be important for clinically sensitive tasks. Incorporating spatial structure into WSI condensation is an important direction for future work. Second, the PPP prior assumes independent concept occurrence. While this is reasonable when concepts represent distinguishable prototypical patterns, it may limit the ability to capture highly complex or correlated morphological structures in extreme cases. Extending NICER with more flexible priors could further improve its expressiveness. Finally, NICER is formulated under a fixed pretrained representation lens. Although we examine the effect of encoder choice using two foundation models, a more systematic evaluation across diverse pretrained encoders would further clarify its robustness, generality, and applicability in real-world medical settings.
